You’re not dumb. Big O stuff is just a way to talk about how the time (or space) grows when your input gets bigger. Let’s break it down in simple terms, then we’ll walk through a few easy examples and a quick amortized example.

Simple metaphor
- Imagine you’re looking for a friend in a line of people.
  - If you always check just the first person and stop, that’s O(1) — constant time.
  - If you have to check everyone once, that’s O(n) — it grows linearly with the number of people.
  - If you can cut the line roughly in half each time and keep going, that’s O(log n) — the number of steps grows with the log of the line length.
  - If you have to check every pair of people in nested loops, that’s O(n^2) — the work grows like n times n.
  - If you sort people with a good algorithm, you often get O(n log n) — a mix of “do something n times” and “do something a bit for each level” (explained below).

What the big O families mean (quick intuition)
- O(1): constant time. No matter how big n is, the same amount of work.
  - Example: Accessing the nth item in an array by index.
- O(log n): logarithmic. Doubling the input nearly just adds one step.
  - Example: Binary search in a sorted array.
- O(n): linear. Work grows in direct proportion to n.
  - Example: Scanning every item once.
- O(n log n): n times log n. Often appears when you do something linear for each of about log n levels, like a good sort.
  - Example: Efficient sorting algorithms like mergesort (rough idea: split in halves log n times, process n items at each level).
- O(n^2): quadratic. Nested loops over n items.
  - Example: A double loop of i = 1..n and j = 1..n.
- O(2^n), O(n!): exponential or factorial. Grows extremely fast; not practical for large n.

Amortized analysis in plain words
- When you look at a sequence of operations, some operations can be expensive, but you average the cost per operation over the whole sequence.
- Think of a piggy bank: you save “credits” for expensive steps and spend them gradually so the average per step stays low.

A classic example: dynamic array pushes
- Idea: You have an array that can grow. Pushing (adding) a new item costs 1 step most of the time.
- But occasionally you run out of space, so you resize the array to be bigger and copy everything over. That one push can seem expensive.
- If you resize by doubling the size when you run out, the expensive copies happen less and less often as you do more pushes.
- The total cost of n pushes is about 2n (not exactly, but up to a constant factor). So the average cost per push is about 2, which is O(1) amortized.
- So: even though some pushes are expensive, the amortized cost per push stays constant.

A quick way to think about amortized costs
- Pick a sequence of ops.
- Assign a little “credit” to cheap ops so you can pay for the occasional expensive one.
- If you can show the total cost over n ops is at most C * n for some constant C, you get O(1) amortized.

Why this matters in homework and interviews
- Big O looks at the leading growth, not exact numbers. We drop constants and less-important terms.
- Often there are several big-O answers possible; we pick the smallest f(n) that still upper-bounds the time for large n.
- Amortized analysis is used when a single operation isn’t always the same cost but the average over many operations is bounded.

Tiny practice problems (try these, quick checks)
- What’s the time complexity of:
  a) A loop for i = 1 to n that does O(1) work inside? -> O(n)
  b) A loop for i = 1 to n, inside it a loop for j = 1 to n? -> O(n^2)
  c) A loop that halves n each time (while n > 1, n = floor(n/2))? -> O(log n)
  d) A sort like mergesort (divide and conquer, processing n items per level, about log n levels)? -> O(n log n)
- Amortized example: push/pop on a dynamic array that doubles when full. If you do n pushes starting from size 1, what’s the amortized cost per push? (Answer: O(1) amortized.)

- If you can prove both an upper bound and a matching lower bound, you’ve got Theta(g(n)) – that’s the tight description of the growth.
- If you only prove an upper bound (O), you know the function doesn’t grow faster than g(n), but it might grow slower (e.g., it could be a lot smaller like sqrt(n) or even a constant). In that case you don’t know the exact asymptotic rate.

- A simple linear scan that sometimes returns early (best case O(1)) but worst-case is O(n) is not tight if you’re talking about the worst-case bound alone. The worst-case bound is O(n), but you can’t say Theta(n) unless you also prove a matching Omega(n) for the worst case. - If you can prove both an upper bound and a matching lower bound, say Theta(g(n)).
- If you only prove an upper bound, say O(g(n)) (not necessarily tight).
- If you’re unsure about the tightness, you can try to also prove a lower bound like Ω(g(n)); if you can, you get Theta(g(n)).

What we’re counting
- Imagine a counter with enough bits to avoid wrapping (so we can keep incrementing).
- Each increment flips some bits from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. The cost of an increment is the number of bits flipped in that step.
- Sometimes you flip just 1 bit (cheap). Sometimes you flip several trailing 1s to 0 and one more 0 to 1 (expensive).

Eight increments example
We’ll use a 4-bit counter, starting at 0000, and do 8 increments. Here are the costs (how many bits flip) for each increment:

- 0000 -> 0001: cost 1
- 0001 -> 0010: cost 2
- 0010 -> 0011: cost 1
- 0011 -> 0100: cost 3
- 0100 -> 0101: cost 1
- 0101 -> 0110: cost 2
- 0110 -> 0111: cost 1
- 0111 -> 1000: cost 4

Total cost for the 8 increments = 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 15
Amortized cost per increment = 15 / 8 ≈ 1.875, which is O(1) amortized.

Why this works (the intuition)
- Most increments flip just one bit (the least significant 0 becomes 1). That’s cheap.
- Occasionally you have a run of trailing 1s: you flip those to 0 (cost equal to how many trailing 1s) and flip the next 0 to 1 (one more flip). This is the expensive step.
- Across many increments, the number of times you pay for those extra flips is bounded. In fact, if you do n increments, the total number of bit flips across all increments is at most 2n. So the average flips per increment is at most 2 (a constant).

Takeaways
- Amortized cost measures the average cost per operation over a sequence, not just one operation.
- In this binary counter example, although some increments are expensive, the expensive work is paid for by many cheap increments, keeping the long-run average constant.
- This is a classic demonstration that amortized analysis can give a much nicer bound than looking at a single worst-case step.

Quick graph basics (recap)
- Graph can be directed or undirected, and edges have weights (non-negative for Dijkstra).
- You often want the shortest path from a source s to every other vertex.
- Distinguish between:
  - BFS: shortest paths in unweighted graphs (or equal-weight edges)
  - Dijkstra: shortest paths with non-negative weights
  - Bellman-Ford: works with negative weights (can detect negative cycles)
  - Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest paths

Dijkstra’s algorithm in plain terms
- You keep a distance estimate for every vertex (dist[v]), starting with dist[s] = 0 and dist[others] = ∞.
- Repeatedly pick the not-yet-finalized vertex with the smallest dist (the closest one you haven’t settled yet).
- Relax its outgoing edges: if going through this vertex gives a shorter path to a neighbor, update that neighbor’s dist and remember the previous node on that best path.
- Use a priority queue (min-heap) to pick the next closest vertex efficiently.
- Important: weights must be non-negative for the standard version.

A clean, compact walk-through with an example graph
Graph (5 nodes: S, A, B, C, D)
Edges (weights):
- S -> A with weight 4
- S -> C with weight 2
- C -> A with weight 1
- C -> D with weight 4
- A -> B with weight 5
- A -> D with weight 2
- D -> B with weight 3
All edges are directed; you can treat an undirected edge as two directed ones if needed.

Goal: shortest paths from S to all nodes.

Step-by-step with the distances and the chosen vertex each time
1) Initialization
- dist[S] = 0
- dist[A] = ∞, dist[C] = ∞, dist[D] = ∞, dist[B] = ∞
- Prev pointers (to reconstruct paths) are all NIL

2) Pick the closest vertex not yet finalized: S (dist 0)
- Relax edges from S:
  - S -> A (4): dist[A] becomes 4, prev[A] = S
  - S -> C (2): dist[C] becomes 2, prev[C] = S
- Distances now: A=4, C=2, D=∞, B=∞

3) Pick the next closest: C (dist 2)
- Relax edges from C:
  - C -> A (1): path S -> C -> A has length 2 + 1 = 3, which is < current dist[A] (4). Update: dist[A] = 3, prev[A] = C
  - C -> D (4): dist[D] becomes 2 + 4 = 6, prev[D] = C
- Distances now: A=3, C=2 (finalized), D=6, B=∞

4) Next closest: A (dist 3)
- Relax edges from A:
  - A -> B (5): dist[B] becomes 3 + 5 = 8, prev[B] = A
  - A -> D (2): path S -> C -> A -> D has length 3 + 2 = 5, which is < current dist[D] (6). Update: dist[D] = 5, prev[D] = A
- Distances now: B=8, D=5

5) Next closest: D (dist 5)
- Relax edges from D:
  - D -> B (3): path S -> ... -> D -> B has length 5 + 3 = 8, which ties with current dist[B] (8). No change (you can choose to tie-break however you like).
- Distances now: B=8

6) Next closest: B (dist 8)
- All done (B has no outgoing edges that improve anything in this example).

Final shortest distances from S:
- S: 0
- A: 3 (path S -> C -> A)
- C: 2 (path S -> C)
- D: 5 (path S -> C -> A -> D)
- B: 8 (path S -> C -> A -> D -> B)

What to remember from this example
- The key idea is the “finalize the closest vertex, then relax its edges” pattern.
- The distances you get are final for a vertex once you pop it from the priority queue (in the standard implementation with a min-heap).
- If there are multiple shortest paths, Dijkstra will pick one depending on tie-breaking.
- Complexity (typical): O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap. With a simple array implementation, it’s O(V^2). For dense graphs E ~ V^2, the dense version can be fine; for sparse graphs the heap version shines.

Common pitfalls and tips
- Weights must be non-negative for the classic Dijkstra. If you have negative weights, consider Bellman-Ford or Johnson’s algorithm (which handles all-pairs with potential reweighting).
- Reconstructing paths: keep a prev[] array so you can backtrack from any target to the source to get the actual path.
- If you’re implementing, remember to handle the “decrease-key” operation efficiently. If your language/runtime doesn’t have it, you can push duplicates with better distances and ignore stale entries when you pop them.
- If you only need the distance to a single target, you can stop early as soon as you pop that target from the queue.

- DFS for connectivity, topological sort (on directed acyclic graphs).
- Bellman-Ford for graphs with negative weights and for detecting negative cycles: O(VE).
- Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs shortest paths: O(V^3) time, simple to implement with dynamic programming.
- Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): Prim’s algorithm (greedy, using a min-heap) or Kruskal’s algorithm (sort edges and union-find). Typical complexities: O((V + E) log V) for Prim with a heap; Kruskal O(E log E) or O(E log V) with a good implementation.

What Bellman-Ford does
- Works on graphs with possibly negative edge weights.
- It relaxes every edge, repeatedly, for V-1 passes (V = number of vertices). This ensures shortest paths are found even if some edges are negative.
- After V-1 passes, if you can still relax any edge, there’s a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.
- Complexity: O(V · E) time, O(V) space.
